interludes.headline: Did You Know?
interludes.text: South Boston's annual St. Patrick's Day parade has been running since 1901, making it one of the oldest in America.

interludes.headline: Local Lore
interludes.text: Castle Island isn't actually an island anymore. It was connected to the mainland in 1928.

interludes.headline: Triple Deckers
interludes.text: The iconic triple-decker homes were built for immigrant families to share, with each floor housing a different generation.

interludes.headline: The Brownies
interludes.text: The L Street Brownies have been swimming in the Atlantic year-round since 1902. Even on January 1st.

interludes.headline: Broadway's Heart
interludes.text: Broadway in Southie was once the center of the Irish immigrant community, lined with bakeries, pubs, and parish halls.

interludes.headline: America's Little Italy
interludes.text: The North End has been Boston's Italian neighborhood since the 1880s, home to over 100 restaurants in just 1 square mile.

interludes.headline: Saint's Days
interludes.text: Every summer, the North End hosts over a dozen religious festivals honoring Italian patron saints, called 'festas.'

interludes.headline: Paul Revere's Ride
interludes.text: Paul Revere's house, built around 1680, is the oldest remaining structure in downtown Boston.

interludes.headline: Narrow Streets
interludes.text: The North End's narrow, winding streets follow the original colonial layout, predating the grid system.

interludes.headline: Cannoli Wars
interludes.text: Mike's Pastry and Modern Pastry have been in a friendly cannoli rivalry since the 1940s. Locals take sides seriously.

interludes.headline: America's Oldest
interludes.text: Fenway Park opened in 1912, making it the oldest Major League Baseball stadium still in use.

interludes.headline: The Green Monster
interludes.text: The Green Monster is 37 feet tall. It was originally built to prevent people from watching games for free.

interludes.headline: Curse Reversed
interludes.text: The 'Curse of the Bambino' lasted 86 years after the Red Sox sold Babe Ruth in 1920. They finally won in 2004.

interludes.headline: Kenmore Square
interludes.text: The iconic Citgo sign has been glowing over Kenmore Square since 1965, becoming an unofficial Boston landmark.

interludes.headline: Pesky's Pole
interludes.text: The right field foul pole is named for Johnny Pesky, though he only hit six home runs around it.

interludes.headline: Gaslight Era
interludes.text: Beacon Hill still has gas-lit street lamps. The 1800s aesthetic is protected by strict historical guidelines.

interludes.headline: Purple Panes
interludes.text: Some Beacon Hill windows have purple glass, accidentally created by manganese oxide reacting with sunlight over centuries.

interludes.headline: Acorn Street
interludes.text: Acorn Street is often called the most photographed street in America. The cobblestones are original.

interludes.headline: The Sacred Cod
interludes.text: A wooden codfish has hung in the Massachusetts State House since 1784, symbolizing the fishing industry's importance.

interludes.headline: Literary Haven
interludes.text: Louisa May Alcott, Nathaniel Hawthorne, and Henry David Thoreau all lived on Beacon Hill.

charlestown.theme: Revolutionary War history and Navy pride

interludes.headline: Old Ironsides
interludes.text: The USS Constitution, launched in 1797, is the world's oldest commissioned warship still afloat.

interludes.headline: Bunker Hill
interludes.text: 'Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes' was supposedly said at the Battle of Bunker Hill in 1775.

interludes.headline: Navy Yard Legacy
interludes.text: The Charlestown Navy Yard built and repaired ships for 174 years, from 1800 to 1974.

interludes.headline: The Monument
interludes.text: The Bunker Hill Monument has 294 steps and no elevator. Climbing it became a Boston rite of passage.

interludes.headline: Townies
interludes.text: Charlestown was a separate town until 1874. Many 'Townies' families have lived there for generations.

interludes.headline: Made Land
interludes.text: Back Bay was literally underwater until the 1850s. It took 40 years to fill in the bay with gravel.

interludes.headline: Alphabetical Order
interludes.text: The cross streets in Back Bay run alphabetically: Arlington, Berkeley, Clarendon, Dartmouth, Exeter, Fairfield, Gloucester, Hereford.

interludes.headline: Copley Square
interludes.text: The Boston Public Library was the first large free municipal library in America, opened in 1895.

interludes.headline: Brownstone Row
interludes.text: Commonwealth Avenue's brownstones were designed to rival the grand boulevards of Paris.

interludes.headline: Trinity Church
interludes.text: Trinity Church sits on 4,500 wooden pilings. Workers must keep them wet to prevent rot.

interludes.headline: Oldest in America
interludes.text: Harvard was founded in 1636, just 16 years after the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth Rock.

interludes.headline: Cambridge Connection
interludes.text: Cambridge, Massachusetts was named after Cambridge, England, where many early colonists had studied.

interludes.headline: Nobel Central
interludes.text: MIT has produced 98 Nobel laureates, making it one of the most decorated research institutions on Earth.

interludes.headline: Harvard Square
interludes.text: Harvard Square has been a gathering place since 1630, predating the university itself.

interludes.headline: The Statue
interludes.text: The John Harvard statue is called the 'Statue of Three Lies' because the name, date, and claim of being the founder are all wrong.

interludes.headline: Dot's Scale
interludes.text: Dorchester is Boston's largest neighborhood by area and population. Locals call it 'Dot.'

interludes.headline: Triple Deckers
interludes.text: Dorchester has more triple-decker homes than any other neighborhood in America.

interludes.headline: JFK's Birthplace
interludes.text: John F. Kennedy was born in Brookline, but Dorchester's JFK/UMass T station honors his family's Boston roots.

interludes.headline: First in America
interludes.text: The first chocolate factory in America opened in Dorchester in 1764. It became Baker's Chocolate.

interludes.headline: Cultural Mosaic
interludes.text: Dorchester is one of the most ethnically diverse zip codes in America, home to Vietnamese, Irish, Haitian, and Cape Verdean communities.

interludes.headline: Freedom Trail
interludes.text: The Freedom Trail covers 2.5 miles and 16 historic sites, from Boston Common to the Bunker Hill Monument.

interludes.headline: Faneuil Hall
interludes.text: Faneuil Hall has been called the 'Cradle of Liberty' since Samuel Adams and others debated independence there.

interludes.headline: Boston Massacre
interludes.text: The Boston Massacre happened on March 5, 1770. A circle of cobblestones marks the spot on State Street.

interludes.headline: Old South Meeting
interludes.text: The Boston Tea Party was planned at Old South Meeting House before 5,000 colonists marched to Griffin's Wharf.

interludes.headline: King's Chapel
interludes.text: King's Chapel was built in 1688 and contains the oldest pulpit still in use in America.

interludes.headline: Innovation District
interludes.text: The Seaport transformed from parking lots to a tech hub in just 15 years, attracting startups and biotech firms.

interludes.headline: Boston Tea Party
interludes.text: Griffin's Wharf, where the Tea Party happened in 1773, was located in what is now the Seaport district.

interludes.headline: ICA Boston
interludes.text: The Institute of Contemporary Art was the first new museum built in Boston in 100 years when it opened in 2006.

interludes.headline: Convention Center
interludes.text: The Boston Convention and Exhibition Center is the largest convention center in the Northeast, covering 2.1 million square feet.

interludes.headline: Harbor Walk
interludes.text: The 43-mile HarborWalk connects beaches, parks, and neighborhoods along Boston's entire waterfront.
